claim: 48 volunteers (mean age 23.6 ± 1.4, 32 females) were recruited for the study.
source: We recruited 48 volunteers (mean age 23.6 ± 1.4, 32 females) to perform a binary lottery task requiring arbitration between individual experienced card outcomes and expert advice.
evidence: Direct statement of participant demographics in the manuscript.

claim: 38 participants (mean age 24.2 ± 1.3; 26 females) entered the final analysis.
source: Altogether, 38 participants (mean age 24.2 ± 1.3; 26 females) entered the final analysis.
evidence: Direct statement of final sample size after exclusions.

claim: Decision confidence, as measured by the number of points participants wagered on their predictions, varied with arbitration defined as a ratio of precisions.
source: Decision confidence, as measured by the number of points participants wagered on their predictions, varied with our definition of arbitration as a ratio of precisions.
evidence: Direct statement from the abstract describing the relationship between wager amount and arbitration.

claim: Arbitrating in favor of self-gathered information activated the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the midbrain.
source: Arbitrating in favor of self-gathered information activated the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the midbrain, whereas arbitrating in favor of social information engaged the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the amygdala.
evidence: Direct statement from the abstract describing neural correlates of arbitration.

claim: Arbitrating in favor of social information engaged the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the amygdala.
source: Arbitrating in favor of self-gathered information activated the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the midbrain, whereas arbitrating in favor of social information engaged the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the amygdala.
evidence: Direct statement from the abstract describing neural correlates of arbitration.

claim: Arbitration signals were independent of decision confidence.
source: Functional neuroimaging demonstrated that arbitration signals were independent of decision confidence and involved modality-specific brain regions.
evidence: Direct statement from the abstract describing the relationship between arbitration and confidence.

claim: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and the frontopolar cortex have been shown to arbitrate between habitual (model-free) and planned (model-based) learning systems.
source: Specifically, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and the frontopolar cortex have been shown to arbitrate between habitual (model-free) and planned (model-based) learning systems (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Lee et al., 2014.

claim: Theory of mind (ToM) processes involve inference about others' mental states.
source: First, arbitration involving social information could rely on theory of mind (ToM) processes, that is inference about others' mental states (Frith and Frith, 2005; Schaafsma et al., 2015) and higher-level social representations (Frith, 2012; Devaine et al., 2014a).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Frith and Frith, 2005 and Schaafsma et al., 2015.

claim: Classical ToM regions include the temporoparietal junction (TPJ) and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex.
source: Accordingly, arbitration involving the intentions of others may rely on activity in classical ToM regions, such as the temporoparietal junction (TPJ) and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Carrington and Bailey, 2009; Frith and Frith, 2010; Baker, 2011; Schurz et al., 2014).

claim: Parts of the striatum including the caudate show stronger activations in response to reciprocated compared to unreciprocated cooperation during iterative trust games.
source: For example, parts of the striatum including the caudate show stronger activations in response to reciprocated compared to unreciprocated cooperation during iterative trust games (Delgado et al., 2005; King-Casas et al., 2008; Fareri et al., 2015), and represent social prediction errors signaling a change in fidelity (Delgado et al., 2005; Biele et al., 2009; Klucharev et al., 2009; Campbell-Meiklejohn et al., 2010; Braams et al., 2014; Diaconescu et al., 2017).

claim: The ACC was shown to represent volatility precision-weighted prediction errors (PEs) during social learning.
source: In addition to being associated with volatility tracking in a probabilistic reward learning task (Behrens et al., 2007), the ACC was shown to represent volatility precision-weighted prediction errors (PEs) during social learning (Diaconescu et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Behrens et al., 2007 and Diaconescu et al., 2017.

claim: Previous studies have implicated dopaminergic, cholinergic, and noradrenergic systems in signaling uncertainty for non-social forms of learning.
source: For non-social forms of learning, previous studies have implicated dopaminergic, cholinergic, and noradrenergic systems in signaling uncertainty, defined as the inverse of precision (Yu and Dayan, 2005; Iglesias et al., 2013; Payzan-LeNestour et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2015; Marshall et al., 2016).

claim: Participants predicted the outcome of a binary lottery using advice from a more informed advisor and information inferred from individually observed card outcomes.
source: Specifically, we examined how people arbitrate between individual reward information and social advice about a probabilistic lottery where contingencies changed over time. Participants learned to predict the outcome of a binary card draw using advice from a more informed advisor and information inferred from individually observed card outcomes (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement describing the task, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The advisor based his or her suggestion on information that was true with a probability of 80%.
source: The advisor based his or her suggestion on information that was true with a probability of 80%, although the participants were not informed of this fact.
evidence: Direct statement describing the advisor's information accuracy.

claim: The average probability of advice being correct was 56% of trials.
source: Furthermore, the advisor received monetary incentives to change his or her strategy and thus provide either helpful or misleading advice at different stages of the game (Figure 1b) with the average probability of advice being correct in 56% of trials.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: The average lottery prediction accuracy across all trials was 68.2 ± 6.2%.
source: The average values across all trials were 68.2 ± 6.2% (mean accuracy ± standard deviation) lottery prediction accuracy, 62.1 ± 6.9% advice-taking, and 5.6 ± 1.5 points wagered (participants on average accumulated 378.6 ± 173.2 points).
evidence: Direct statement in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption.

claim: Participants took advice 62.1 ± 6.9% of the time on average.
source: The average values across all trials were 68.2 ± 6.2% (mean accuracy ± standard deviation) lottery prediction accuracy, 62.1 ± 6.9% advice-taking, and 5.6 ± 1.5 points wagered (participants on average accumulated 378.6 ± 173.2 points).
evidence: Direct statement in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption.

claim: Participants wagered an average of 5.6 ± 1.5 points per trial.
source: The average values across all trials were 68.2 ± 6.2% (mean accuracy ± standard deviation) lottery prediction accuracy, 62.1 ± 6.9% advice-taking, and 5.6 ± 1.5 points wagered (participants on average accumulated 378.6 ± 173.2 points).
evidence: Direct statement in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption.

claim: Participants accumulated an average of 378.6 ± 173.2 points.
source: The average values across all trials were 68.2 ± 6.2% (mean accuracy ± standard deviation) lottery prediction accuracy, 62.1 ± 6.9% advice-taking, and 5.6 ± 1.5 points wagered (participants on average accumulated 378.6 ± 173.2 points).
evidence: Direct statement in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption.

claim: Lottery prediction accuracy showed a main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 187.94, p = 7.7e-16).
source: First, for the accuracy with which participants predicted lottery outcome, we found a main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 187.94, p = 7.7e-16) and an information source-by-phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 11.13, p = 0.0020) (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Lottery prediction accuracy showed an information source-by-phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 11.13, p = 0.0020).
source: First, for the accuracy with which participants predicted lottery outcome, we found a main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 187.94, p = 7.7e-16) and an information source-by-phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 11.13, p = 0.0020) (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Participants performed significantly better in stable compared to volatile periods of the task.
source: Thus, in-keeping with the rationale that arbitration relates to relative information quality, the degree to which participants relied on each information source was a function of precision as manipulated using the volatility structure of the task. Participants performed significantly better in stable compared to volatile periods of the task.

claim: Advice-taking behavior showed a main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 56.26, p=7.3073e-09).
source: Second, advice-taking behavior differed as a function of volatility and information source: For the percentage of trials in which participants followed a given source of information, we detected a main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 56.26, p=7.3073e-09) and an information source-by-phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 25.86, p=1.1561e-05) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Advice-taking behavior showed an information source-by-phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 25.86, p=1.1561e-05).
source: Second, advice-taking behavior differed as a function of volatility and information source: For the percentage of trials in which participants followed a given source of information, we detected a main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 56.26, p=7.3073e-09) and an information source-by-phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 25.86, p=1.1561e-05) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Participants took advice less often particularly when it was volatile rather than stable.
source: Thus, participants took advice less often particularly when it was volatile rather than stable.

claim: The amount of points wagered showed a main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 28.78, p = 4.54e-06).
source: Third, the amount of points wagered also depended on the task volatility and the information source. We observed a main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 28.78, p = 4.54e-06) and an information source-by-phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 16.75, p = 2.21e-04; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: The amount of points wagered showed an information source-by-phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 16.75, p = 2.21e-04).
source: Third, the amount of points wagered also depended on the task volatility and the information source. We observed a main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 28.78, p = 4.54e-06) and an information source-by-phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 16.75, p = 2.21e-04; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Participants wagered fewer points particularly when advice was volatile.
source: Participants wagered fewer points particularly when advice was volatile.

claim: A hypothetical person who did not take the volatility of the task phases into account gained on average 21.6 points less than an agent tracking volatility.
source: Simulations using a two-level HGF (with low and fixed volatility) suggested that tracking volatility is beneficial for task performance: a hypothetical person who did not take the volatility of the task phases into account gained on average 21.6 points less than an agent tracking volatility.

claim: Participants rated the advice as 75.0 ± 4.6% helpful in the stable advice phase.
source: On average, participants rated the advice as 75.0 ± 4.6% (mean ± standard deviation) helpful in the stable advice phase.
evidence: Direct statement of advisor rating results.

claim: Participants rated the advice as 50 ± 3.4% helpful in the volatile advice phase.
source: The corresponding values were 50 ± 3.4% in the volatile advice phase, 63.8 ± 4.4% in the stable card phase, and 61.2 ± 3.8% in the volatile card phase.
evidence: Direct statement of advisor rating results.

claim: Advice ratings showed a significant main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 15.67, p = 3.3e-04).
source: We examined the extent to which participants' ratings changed as a function of the task phases, and found a significant main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 15.67, p = 3.3e-04) and a significant information source × phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 8.42, p = 0.0062).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Advice ratings showed a significant information source × phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 8.42, p = 0.0062).
source: We examined the extent to which participants' ratings changed as a function of the task phases, and found a significant main effect of phase (df = (1,36), F = 15.67, p = 3.3e-04) and a significant information source × phase interaction (df = (1,36), F = 8.42, p = 0.0062).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Advice ratings decreased during volatile compared to stable phases, and this effect was more strongly related to the advice compared to the card information.
source: This suggests that advice ratings decreased during volatile compared to stable phases, and this effect was more strongly related to the advice compared to the card information.

claim: Thirty out of 38 participants answered 'Yes' to whether the advisor intentionally used a strategy during the task.
source: Thirty out of 38 participants answered 'Yes' to this question, and described (in their own words) the advisor's strategy.
evidence: Direct statement of debriefing questionnaire results.

claim: Participants rated the advisors' recommendations as helpful with mean ratings of 4.2 ± 1.0 on a 6-point Likert scale.
source: In general, participants rated the advisors' recommendations as helpful (mean ratings 4.2 ± 1.0, ranging from 2 to 6).
evidence: Direct statement of debriefing questionnaire results.

claim: Participants reported that they followed the advice 60% of the time on average (mean ratings 60 ± 12).
source: On average, participants reported that they followed the advice 60% of the time (mean ratings 60 ± 12), which significantly differed from chance (t(37) = 5.02, p=1.29e-05).
evidence: Direct statement of debriefing questionnaire results.

claim: Participants' self-reported advice-following significantly differed from chance (t(37) = 5.02, p=1.29e-05).
source: On average, participants reported that they followed the advice 60% of the time (mean ratings 60 ± 12), which significantly differed from chance (t(37) = 5.02, p=1.29e-05).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Participants learned similarly from individual (volatile card probabilities) and social (advisor fidelity) information.
source: This result suggests that participants learned similarly from individual (volatile card probabilities) and social (advisor fidelity) information.
evidence: Direct statement of interpretation of results.

claim: The social bias parameter ζ differed significantly from zero (t(36) = 5.09, p=1.07e-05).
source: The reliability-independent social bias parameter ζ differed significantly from zero (t(36) = 5.09, p=1.07e-05).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: On average, participants relied more on the advisor's recommendations compared to their own sampling of the card outcomes.
source: Thus, on average, participants relied more on the advisor's recommendations compared to their own sampling of the card outcomes (Figure 4c).
evidence: Direct statement of behavioral results with reference to Figure 4c.

claim: The stronger the bias to arbitrate in favor of social information, the more points participants wagered.
source: The stronger the bias to arbitrate in favor of social information, the more points participants wagered.

claim: The higher the estimated advisor volatility, the fewer points participants were willing to wager on a given trial.
source: Conversely, estimated advisor volatility was negatively associated with the amount wagered: the higher the estimated advisor volatility, the fewer points participants were willing to wager on a given trial (see Table 2 for the priors over the parameters, Table 1b for all parameter estimates, and Figure 5 for the trial-wise influence of the average computational quantities on wager amount).

claim: Advice helpfulness ratings were explained by model parameter estimates (R2 = 32.2%, F = 2.46, p=0.04).
source: Moreover, advice helpfulness ratings were explained by model parameter estimates (R2 = 32.2%, F = 2.46, p=0.04).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Hierarchical precision-weighted PE signals were replicated in the same dopaminergic and frontoparietal regions as in previous studies using other sensory and social learning domains.
source: Hierarchical precision-weighted PE signals were replicated in the same dopaminergic and frontoparietal regions as in previous studies using other sensory and social learning domains (see Iglesias et al., 2013; Diaconescu et al., 2017), indicating that the modifications in the experimental paradigm did not affect basic learning processes (see Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Direct statement with citations and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Undirected tests for arbitration activity identified ventral prefrontal regions, such as the left ventromedial PFC (peak at [-2, 46,–10]) and the right orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) [26, 34, -10].
source: Undirected tests for arbitration activity identified ventral prefrontal regions, such as the left ventromedial PFC (peak at [-2, 46,–10]) and the right orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) [26, 34, -10].

claim: Frontal activations for arbitration included the right frontopolar cortex [4, 54, 30] and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC) [50, 36, 0].
source: Interestingly, frontal activations also included the right frontopolar cortex [4, 54, 30] and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC) [50, 36, 0], regions previously associated with arbitration between model-based and model-free forms of individual learning (Lee et al., 2014; Figure 6).
evidence: Direct statement of fMRI results with citation.

claim: The right VLPFC showing arbitration-related effects at [48, 35, -2] significantly overlapped with the arbitration-related reliability activations detected by Lee and colleagues.
source: The right VLPFC showing arbitration-related effects at [48, 35, -2] significantly overlapped with the arbitration-related reliability activations detected by Lee and colleagues, supporting the notion that arbitration is to some extent domain-independent.
evidence: Direct statement of fMRI results with reference to Lee et al.

claim: A wide network of cortical and subcortical regions contributes to arbitration including occipital areas, the anterior insula, left thalamus, left putamen, bilateral middle cingulate sulcus, supplementary motor area (SMA) [−2, -8, 52], left dorsal middle cingulate gyrus [−10,–26, 44], the right amygdala [18, -10, -16] and the left midbrain [−6,–18, −12].
source: In addition, we found that a wide network of cortical and subcortical regions contributes to arbitration that included occipital areas, the anterior insula, left thalamus, left putamen, bilateral middle cingulate sulcus, supplementary motor area (SMA) [−2, -8, 52], left dorsal middle cingulate gyrus [−10,–26, 44], the right amygdala [18, -10, -16] and the left midbrain [−6,–18, −12] (Table 3, Figure 6).

claim: Directed tests for arbitration in favor of individual over social information identified activity increases in the right dorsolateral PFC [36, 46, 30], left SMA/anterior cingulate sulcus [−2,–8, 52] and the midbrain [−6,–18,−12].
source: Directed tests for arbitration in favor of individual over social information identified activity increases in the right dorsolateral PFC [36, 46, 30], left SMA/anterior cingulate sulcus [−2,–8, 52] and the midbrain [−6,–18,−12] (Figure 7a).

claim: Primarily dorsal regions of PFC were modulated by arbitration in favor of individually estimated card probability.
source: In summary, primarily dorsal regions of PFC were modulated by arbitration in favor of individually estimated card probability.

claim: Activity in the right amygdala, VLPFC, orbitofrontal and ventromedial PFC was modulated by arbitration in favor of the advisor's suggestions.
source: Conversely, activity in the right amygdala, VLPFC, orbitofrontal and ventromedial PFC was modulated by arbitration in favor of the advisor's suggestions (Figure 7b).

claim: The right anterior TPJ [56, -52, 24], right superior temporal gyrus [52, -18, -8], and right precuneus [6, -51, 32] showed increased activity during arbitration in favor of social information.
source: Outside PFC, the right anterior TPJ [56, -52, 24], right superior temporal gyrus [52, -18, -8], and right precuneus [6, -51, 32] showed similar effects (Tables 4 and 5 for the entire list of brain regions).

claim: Primarily ventral regions of PFC together with temporal and parietal regions were more active during arbitration in favor of social information.
source: Thus, primarily ventral regions of PFC together with temporal and parietal regions were more active during arbitration in favor of social information.

claim: A single cluster in the right substantia nigra survived small-volume correction (p<0.05 FWE voxel-level corrected for the entire ROI; peak at [−6,–18, −12]).
source: A single cluster in the right substantia nigra survived small-volume correction (p<0.05 FWE voxel-level corrected for the entire ROI; peak at [−6,–18, −12]; Figure 8).
evidence: Direct statement of ROI analysis results.

claim: Activity in the substantia nigra increased with arbitration in favor of individual estimates of card probabilities rather than advice.
source: Activity in this region increased with arbitration in favor of individual estimates of card probabilities rather than advice.

claim: Regions showing arbitration effects had significantly larger effects of arbitration than of the amount of points wagered.
source: It is important to note that these regions showed significantly larger effects of arbitration than of the amount of points wagered.

claim: Responses reflecting arbitration dominated over responses reflecting wager amount in cerebellar, midbrain, occipital, parietal, medial prefrontal, and temporal regions including the amygdala.
source: Responses reflecting arbitration dominated over responses reflecting wager amount in cerebellar, midbrain, occipital, parietal, medial prefrontal, and temporal regions including the amygdala.

claim: Activity in precuneus and ventromedial prefrontal cortex correlated with wager amount.
source: Activity in precuneus and ventromedial prefrontal cortex in turn correlated with wager amount (Figure 9).

claim: Arbitration signals arise on top of decision value and confidence.
source: As wager amount can be taken as a proxy for decision value or confidence (Lebreton et al., 2015), these data suggest that arbitration signals arise on top of decision value and confidence.
evidence: Statement with citation to Lebreton et al., 2015.

claim: A main effect of task phase (i.e. stability/volatility) was found in the factorial analysis.
source: We found two significant results (Figure 10b): (i) a main effect of task phase (i.e. stability/volatility), and (ii) a significant interaction of task phase with source of information.
evidence: Direct statement of factorial analysis results.

claim: A significant interaction of task phase with source of information was found in the factorial analysis.
source: We found two significant results (Figure 10b): (i) a main effect of task phase (i.e. stability/volatility), and (ii) a significant interaction of task phase with source of information.
evidence: Direct statement of factorial analysis results.

claim: The right supramarginal gyrus, bilateral inferior occipital gyri, postcentral/precentral gyri, and the right anterior insula were more active for stable compared to volatile periods.
source: By contrasting stable against volatile phases, irrespective of information source, we found that the right supramarginal gyrus, bilateral inferior occipital gyri, postcentral/precentral gyri, and the right anterior insula were more active for stable compared to volatile periods.

claim: An interaction between task phase and information source showed preferential activity for stable card information in the midbrain [−4,–22, −8].
source: Furthermore, an interaction between task phase and information source showed preferential activity for stable card information in the midbrain [−4,–22, −8].

claim: Additional activations for the interaction between task phase and information source were detected in the right OFC, VLPFC, dorsomedial cingulate gyrus, and anterior cingulate sulcus/SMA.
source: Additional activations were detected in the right OFC, VLPFC, dorsomedial cingulate gyrus, and anterior cingulate sulcus/SMA (Figure 10; Table 6 and Table 7).

claim: These regions processed stability (vs. volatility) more strongly for card than advice information.
source: These regions processed stability (vs. volatility) more strongly for card than advice information.

claim: The regions processing stability (vs. volatility) more strongly for advice than card information overlapped with the arbitration signal, and included the amygdala, the superior temporal sulcus, and the ventromedial PFC.
source: Importantly, the regions processing stability (vs. volatility) more strongly for advice than card information also overlapped with the arbitration signal, and included the amygdala, the superior temporal sulcus, and the ventromedial PFC (Figure 11).

claim: Model-dependent and model-independent analyses agree in localizing arbitration to frontoparietal regions in the individual domain and to ventromedial prefrontal and amygdala regions in the social domain.
source: Thus, model-dependent and model-independent analyses agree in localizing arbitration to frontoparietal regions in the individual domain and to ventromedial prefrontal and amygdala regions in the social domain.

claim: Increased effects of non-social compared to social weighting were detected in bilateral cerebellum, occipital cortices (lingual gyrus, superior occipital cortex), left anterior cingulate sulcus, right supramarginal gyrus, and left postcentral gyrus.
source: Increased effects of non-social compared to social weighting were detected in bilateral cerebellum, occipital cortices (lingual gyrus, superior occipital cortex), left anterior cingulate sulcus, right supramarginal gyrus, and left postcentral gyrus.

claim: Increased representations of social compared to non-social weighting were found in the left subgenual ACC with a maximum at [−7, 36,–11].
source: Conversely, we found increased representations of social compared to non-social weighting in the left subgenual ACC with a maximum at [−7, 36,–11] (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: The outcome-related BOLD activity of the substantia nigra positively correlated with the unsigned precision-weighted outcome PE.
source: Replicating the previous study (Iglesias et al., 2013), we found that the outcome-related BOLD activity of the substantia nigra positively correlated with the unsigned precision-weighted outcome PE, as did the bilateral inferior/middle occipital gyri, anterior insula, (ventro)lateral PFC, and the intraparietal sulcus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Direct statement of fMRI results with citation.

claim: Effects of signed precision-weighted advice PE were detected in right VTA/substantia nigra, the right insula, left middle temporal cortex, right dorsolateral, left dorsomedial and middle frontal cortex.
source: With respect to the signed precision-weighted advice PE (Equation 8), we also replicated results from another recent study (Diaconescu et al., 2017) that employed a different advice-taking paradigm, where participants learned about advice and integrated it along with unambiguous individual information to predict the outcome of a binary lottery. Effects of signed precision-weighted advice PE were detected in right VTA/substantia nigra, the right insula, left middle temporal cortex, right dorsolateral, left dorsomedial and middle frontal cortex (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Direct statement of fMRI results with citation.

claim: Effects of precision-weighted volatility PEs for card outcomes were represented in the right superior temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, and posterior insula.
source: Effects of precision-weighted volatility PEs for card outcomes were represented in the right superior temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, and posterior insula (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a) while the effects of precision-weighted volatility PEs for the adviser fidelity were encoded in the right anterior supplementary motor area (SMA) and anterior insula.

claim: Effects of precision-weighted volatility PEs for the adviser fidelity were encoded in the right anterior supplementary motor area (SMA) and anterior insula.
source: Effects of precision-weighted volatility PEs for card outcomes were represented in the right superior temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, and posterior insula (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a) while the effects of precision-weighted volatility PEs for the adviser fidelity were encoded in the right anterior supplementary motor area (SMA) and anterior insula.

claim: Effects of advice volatility precision-weighted PEs were observed in the cholinergic nuclei in the tegmentum of the brainstem, that is, the pedunculopontine tegmental (PPT) and laterodorsal tegmental (LDT) nuclei (p<0.05 FWE voxel-level within an anatomical mask including all cholinergic nuclei).
source: Finally, we also replicated the finding that higher-level, volatility PEs (Equations 13 and 15) were represented in cholinergic regions. This time, however, we observed effects of advice volatility precision-weighted PEs in the cholinergic nuclei in the tegmentum of the brainstem, that is, the pedunculopontine tegmental (PPT) and laterodorsal tegmental (LDT) nuclei (p<0.05 FWE voxel-level within an anatomical mask including all cholinergic nuclei) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2b).

claim: Participants arbitrated between the two information sources by taking into account their relative precision.
source: Our study shows how healthy participants arbitrate between uncertain social and individual information under varying conditions of stability during a binary lottery task. (Figure 1). Participants arbitrated between the two information sources by taking into account their relative precision.

claim: The more precise one information source was over the other and the more stable the advisor was perceived to be, the more points participants were willing to wager.
source: The more precise one information source was over the other and the more stable the advisor was perceived to be, the more points participants were willing to wager.

claim: Participants tracked the volatility of both the advice and the card color probabilities.
source: By showing that participants tracked the volatility of both the advice and the card color probabilities (Figure 3), our study underscores the importance of volatility in arbitrating between social advice and individual reward-relevant information.

claim: In stable compared to volatile environments, the propensity for arbitration in favor of the more precise information source increases.
source: Thus, in stable compared to volatile environments, the propensity for arbitration in favor of the more precise information source increases.

claim: Numerous studies have demonstrated an important role of volatility in higher level learning.
source: Numerous studies have demonstrated an important role of volatility in higher level learning (Behrens et al., 2007; Behrens et al., 2008; Nassar et al., 2010; Iglesias et al., 2013; Vossel et al., 2014; Diaconescu et al., 2017; Pulcu and Browning, 2017), in-keeping with the present findings.

claim: Arbitration activity in the prefrontal cortex followed a self-versus-other axis: dorsal prefrontal activity increased the more strongly participants weighed their own predictions of reward probabilities over the perceived reliability of the advisor.
source: Note though that arbitration activity in the prefrontal cortex followed a self-versus-other axis: dorsal prefrontal activity increased the more strongly participants weighed their own predictions of reward probabilities over the perceived reliability of the advisor.

claim: Activity in the ventromedial PFC and orbitofrontal cortex showed the opposite pattern and increased in activity as participants relied more heavily on their own reward probability estimates relative to the advice.
source: Conversely, activity in the ventromedial PFC and orbitofrontal cortex showed the opposite pattern and increased in activity as participants relied more heavily on their own reward probability estimates relative to the advice (Figure 7).

claim: Arbitration appears to be sensitive to the source of information entering the arbitration process, contrary to an entirely domain-general process.
source: Together, arbitration appears to be sensitive to the source of information entering the arbitration process, contrary to an entirely domain-general process.

claim: Primate studies found that sustained dopamine neuron activity signaled expected uncertainty.
source: Primate studies found that sustained dopamine neuron activity signaled expected uncertainty (Fiorillo et al., 2003; Schultz, 2010; Schultz et al., 2008).

claim: Human pharmacological studies support the involvement of dopamine in uncertainty coding.
source: This was further supported by human pharmacological studies (Burke et al., 2018; Ojala et al., 2018) as well as fMRI research showing possible involvement of dopamine in risk taking and of dopaminoceptive regions, such as the caudate, anterior insula, ACC and the medial PFC in uncertainty coding (e.g. Dreher et al., 2006; Preuschoff et al., 2008; Tobler et al., 2009) and social advice predictions under uncertainty (Henco et al., 2020).

claim: Studies employing hierarchical Bayesian models have identified ventral tegmental area/substantia nigra activation correlated to precision of predictions about desired outcomes.
source: In particular, studies employing hierarchical Bayesian models have identified ventral tegmental area/substantia nigra activation correlated to precision of predictions about desired outcomes (Friston et al., 2014; Schwartenbeck et al., 2015).

claim: Meta-learning models propose an important role of phasic dopamine signals in training prefrontal system dynamics, to infer on the statistical structure of the environment.
source: Potential neurobiological mechanisms include meta-learning models, which propose an important role of phasic dopamine signals in training prefrontal system dynamics, to infer on the statistical structure of the environment (Collins and Frank, 2016; Wang et al., 2018).

claim: The amygdala has been implicated in processing facial expressions related to affective ToM.
source: The amygdala has been implicated in processing facial expressions related to affective ToM (Schmitgen et al., 2016) and more generally, processing affective value and motivational significance of various stimuli, including other people (Güroğlu et al., 2008; Zink et al., 2008; Zerubavel et al., 2015).

claim: The amygdala may represent the uncertainty of socially-relevant stimuli, inferred from processing the intentions of others.
source: Together these findings suggest that the amygdala may represent the uncertainty of socially-relevant stimuli, inferred from processing the intentions of others.
evidence: Statement based on inference from cited findings.

claim: The orbitofrontal cortex and other areas of the social brain evolved to enable primates and particularly humans to successfully navigate complex social situations.
source: This finding is consistent with the hypothesis that the orbitofrontal cortex and other areas of the social brain evolved to enable primates and particularly humans to successfully navigate complex social situations (Dunbar, 2009).

claim: Strong positive correlations exist between orbitofrontal cortex grey matter volume and social network size.
source: This notion received support from strong positive correlations between orbitofrontal cortex grey matter volume and social network size (Powell et al., 2012), as well as sociocognitive abilities (Powell et al., 2010; Scheuerecker et al., 2010).

claim: The orbitofrontal cortex plays a role in mental state attribution for ambiguous social stimuli.
source: Furthermore, in-keeping with a role of orbitofrontal cortex in mental state attribution for ambiguous social stimuli (Deuse et al., 2016), our findings suggest that this region reduces the uncertainty of social cues that signal changes in intentionality.

claim: The sulcus of the ACC represents predictions related to one's own estimates of the card color outcomes.
source: With respect to social learning signatures, we observed that the sulcus of the ACC represents predictions related to one's own estimates of the card color outcomes, whereas the subgenual ACC represents predictions about the advisor's fidelity.

claim: The subgenual ACC represents predictions about the advisor's fidelity.
source: With respect to social learning signatures, we observed that the sulcus of the ACC represents predictions related to one's own estimates of the card color outcomes, whereas the subgenual ACC represents predictions about the advisor's fidelity.

claim: The sulcus of ACC dorsal to the gyrus plays a domain-general role in motivation.
source: This is consistent with previous findings that the sulcus of ACC dorsal to the gyrus plays a domain-general role in motivation (Rushworth et al., 2007; Rushworth and Behrens, 2008; Apps et al., 2016), whereas the gyrus of the ACC signals information related to other people (Behrens et al., 2008; Apps et al., 2013; Apps et al., 2016; Lockwood, 2016).

claim: The gyrus of the ACC signals information related to other people.
source: This is consistent with previous findings that the sulcus of ACC dorsal to the gyrus plays a domain-general role in motivation (Rushworth et al., 2007; Rushworth and Behrens, 2008; Apps et al., 2016), whereas the gyrus of the ACC signals information related to other people (Behrens et al., 2008; Apps et al., 2013; Apps et al., 2016; Lockwood, 2016).

claim: Individuals with autism spectrum disorder may preferentially rely on their own experiences rather than on the recommendations of others.
source: For example, individuals with autism spectrum disorder may preferentially rely on their own experiences rather than on the recommendations of others.

claim: Individuals with autism appear to represent social prediction errors less strongly than individuals without autism.
source: Indeed, they appear to represent social prediction errors less strongly than individuals without autism (Balsters et al., 2017).

claim: Patients with schizophrenia may be overly confident about their ability to judge advice validity due to fixed beliefs about the advisor's intentions.
source: In contrast, patients with schizophrenia may be overly confident about their ability to judge advice validity due to fixed beliefs about the advisor's intentions (Freeman and Garety, 2014) or show an over-reliance on social information in line with accounts of over-mentalization in this disorder (Montag et al., 2011; Andreou et al., 2015).

claim: The study did not include reciprocal social interactions, but rather used pre-recorded videos of human partners.
source: One limitation of our study is that it did not include reciprocal social interactions, but rather used pre-recorded videos of human partners.

claim: ToM processes may be more prominent in interactive paradigms.
source: ToM processes may be more prominent in interactive paradigms (Diaconescu et al., 2014) or interactions that involve higher levels of recursive thinking (Devaine et al., 2014a; Devaine et al., 2014b).

claim: The study may have limited generalizability to real-world social interactions.
source: By extension, our study may have limited generalizability to real-world social interactions.

claim: Assessing arbitration between social and individual information necessitated the standardization of the advice given to each participant.
source: However, assessing arbitration between social and individual information necessitated the standardization of the advice given to each participant.

claim: The videos of the advisor were extracted from trials when they truly intended to help or truly intended to mislead to make the task as close as possible to a realistic social exchange.
source: To make the task as close as possible to a realistic social exchange, the videos of the advisor were extracted from trials when they truly intended to help or truly intended to mislead.

claim: The study did not include a non-social control task.
source: Second, we did not include a non-social control task.

claim: It is unclear how 'social' the presently investigated form of learning about the advisor's fidelity and volatility actually is.
source: Thus, it is unclear how 'social' the presently investigated form of learning about the advisor's fidelity and volatility actually is.

claim: The differences in activated regions suggest that participants processed the two sources of information differently.
source: The differences in activated regions at least suggest that our participants processed the two sources of information differently.

claim: Whether the process identified is specifically social in nature or rather reflects learning from an indirect information source needs to be examined in future studies by including an additional control condition.
source: However, whether the process we identified is specifically social in nature or rather reflects learning from an indirect information source needs to be examined in future studies by including an additional control condition.
evidence: Direct statement of future research direction.

claim: In a previous control task where the advisor was blindfolded and provided advice with cards from predefined decks, participants did not incorporate time-varying estimates of volatility about the advisor into their decisions.
source: In order to distinguish general inference processes under volatility from inference specific to intentionality, we previously included a control task (Diaconescu et al., 2014), in which the advisor was blindfolded and provided advice with cards from predefined decks that were probabilistically congruent to the actual card color. This control task closely resembled the main task, with the exception of the role of intentionality. Model selection results suggested that participants in the control task did not incorporate time-varying estimates of volatility about the advisor into their decisions.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In the current study, models without volatility performed substantially worse than models with volatility.
source: In the current study, we tested this by including models without volatility, but found that they performed substantially worse than models with volatility (see Figure 2 and Table 2a for details).
evidence: Direct statement of model comparison results.

claim: Participants appeared to process advisor intentionality.
source: Thus, our participants appeared to process advisor intentionality.

claim: Arbitrating between social and individual sources of information corresponds to weighing the relative reliability of each source.
source: Our study indicates that arbitrating between social and individual sources of information corresponds to weighing the relative reliability of each source.

claim: The arbitration process appears to engage different brain regions for social and individual information, in-keeping with domain specificity.
source: This process appears to engage different brain regions for social and individual information, in-keeping with domain specificity.

claim: The lateral prefrontal cortex appears to adjudicate between several different types of learning, in-keeping with domain generality.
source: However, the lateral prefrontal cortex appears to adjudicate between several different types of learning, in-keeping with domain generality.

claim: These findings contribute to our understanding of arbitration in neurotypical individuals, which may provide a knowledge basis for future insight into disorders with impaired arbitration.
source: These findings contribute to our understanding of arbitration in neurotypical individuals, which may provide a knowledge basis for future insight into disorders with impaired arbitration.
evidence: Direct statement of main conclusion and implications.

claim: Participants were non-smokers, right-handed, and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: We recruited 48 volunteers (mean age 23.6 ± 1.4, 32 females) who were non-smokers, right-handed, and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.

claim: Participants had no history of neurological or psychiatric illness, or of drug abuse.
source: Participants had no history of neurological or psychiatric illness, or of drug abuse.

claim: Participants were asked to abstain from alcohol 24 hr prior to the study and from medication, including aspirin, 3 days prior to the study.
source: Participants were asked to abstain from alcohol 24 hr prior to the study and from medication, including aspirin, 3 days prior to the study.

claim: Psychology students were excluded from participation because of previous exposure to similar advice-taking paradigms in their courses.
source: Psychology students were excluded from participation because of previous exposure to similar advice-taking paradigms in their courses.

claim: Data from 10 participants were not analyzed: two pilot participants; one participant who stopped the experiment midway due to head pain; one participant who fell asleep; and six participants where stimulus presentation malfunctioned during the experiment.
source: We did not analyse the data of 10 participants: two pilot participants; one participant who stopped the experiment midway due to head pain; one participant who fell asleep; and six participants where stimulus presentation malfunctioned during the experiment.

claim: Each participant received the same input sequence, that is order and type of videos.
source: To compare participants in terms of their learning and decision-making parameters, we needed to standardize the advice. This means that each participant received the same input sequence,that is order and type of videos.

claim: All video clips were matched in terms of their luminance, contrast, and color balance using Adobe Photoshop Premiere CS6.
source: All video clips were matched in terms of their luminance, contrast, and color balance using Adobe Photoshop Premiere CS6.

claim: Advisor-to-participant assignment was randomized (within the gender-matching constraint) and balanced.
source: Advisor-to-participant assignment was randomized (within the gender-matching constraint) and balanced.

claim: No differences in performance and degree of reliance on advice were found between the four advisors: F(1,36) = 1.82, p=0.16.
source: We found no differences in performance and degree of reliance on advice between the four advisors: F(1,36) = 1.82, p=0.16.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: The tick mark on the wager bar was randomly positioned in each trial to avoid providing a reference point.
source: The tick mark on the wager bar was randomly positioned in each trial to avoid providing a reference point (a regression analysis confirmed that the starting position of the wager indeed failed to explain each participant's trial-wise wager selection, t(37) = −0.89, p=0.31).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design with statistical confirmation.

claim: The starting position of the wager failed to explain each participant's trial-wise wager selection (t(37) = −0.89, p=0.31).
source: The tick mark on the wager bar was randomly positioned in each trial to avoid providing a reference point (a regression analysis confirmed that the starting position of the wager indeed failed to explain each participant's trial-wise wager selection, t(37) = −0.89, p=0.31).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Depending on the correctness of the prediction, the wager was added to or subtracted from the cumulative score and thereby affected the participant's payment at the end of the experiment.
source: Depending on the correctness of the prediction, the wager was added to or subtracted from the cumulative score and thereby affected the participant's payment at the end of the experiment (see below).

claim: The color-to-button assignment used to convey the lottery prediction (blue or green) and the orientation of the wager bar were randomized between participants to prevent confounding with visuomotor processes.
source: The color-to-button assignment used to convey the lottery prediction (blue or green) and the orientation of the wager bar were randomized between participants to prevent confounding with visuomotor processes.

claim: The probability distributions of the two information sources – card color and advice – were designed to be statistically independent.
source: In other words, the probability distributions of the two information sources – card color and advice – were designed to be statistically independent.

claim: The task allowed for a 2 × 2 factorial design structure, where trials could be divided into four conditions: (i) stable card and stable advisor, (ii) stable card and volatile advisor, (iii) volatile card and stable advisor, and (iv) volatile card and volatile advisor in a total of 160 trials.
source: This allowed for a 2 × 2 factorial design structure, where trials could be divided into four conditions: (i) stable card and stable advisor, (ii) stable card and volatile advisor, (iii) volatile card and stable advisor, and (iv) volatile card and volatile advisor in a total of 160 trials (Figure 1b).

claim: The first session included 70 trials and the second session 90 trials.
source: The first session included 70 trials and the second session 90 trials.

claim: Participants could earn a bonus of 10 Swiss Francs for a cumulative score of at least 380 points, and a bonus of 20 Swiss Francs for winning more than 600 points.
source: Participants could earn a bonus of 10 Swiss Francs for a cumulative score of at least 380 points, and a bonus of 20 Swiss Francs for winning more than 600 points.

claim: Participants were not given any information about the bonus thresholds in order to prevent induction of local risk-seeking or risk-averse wagering behavior (reference point effects) when participants were close to a threshold.
source: Importantly, participants were not given any information about the bonus thresholds in order to prevent induction of local risk-seeking or risk-averse wagering behavior (reference point effects) when participants were close to a threshold.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design rationale.

claim: Participants on average reached the first reward bonus and were paid 82.3 ± 8.4 Swiss Francs (including the performance-dependent bonus) at the end of the study.
source: Participants on average reached the first reward bonus and were paid 82.3 ± 8.4 Swiss Francs (including the performance-dependent bonus) at the end of the study.

claim: Functional magnetic resonance images (fMRI) were acquired from a Philips Achieva 3T whole-body scanner with an 8-channel SENSE head coil at the Laboratory for Social Neural Systems Research at the University Hospital Zurich.
source: We acquired functional magnetic resonance images (fMRI) from a Philips Achieva 3T whole-body scanner with an 8-channel SENSE head coil (Philips Medical Systems, Best, The Netherlands) at the Laboratory for Social Neural Systems Research at the University Hospital Zurich.
evidence: Direct statement of data acquisition details.

claim: The first five volumes of each session were discarded to allow for magnetic saturation.
source: The first five volumes of each session were discarded to allow for magnetic saturation.
evidence: Direct statement of data acquisition procedure.

claim: The entire experiment comprised 1300 volumes, with 600 volumes in the first session and 700 in the second.
source: The entire experiment comprised 1300 volumes, with 600 volumes in the first session and 700 in the second.
evidence: Direct statement of data acquisition details.

claim: Heart rate and breathing of the participants were recorded for physiological noise correction purposes using ECG and a pneumatic belt, respectively.
source: Heart rate and breathing of the participants were recorded for physiological noise correction purposes using ECG and a pneumatic belt, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of data acquisition procedure.

claim: The software package SPM12 version 6470 was used to analyse the fMRI data.
source: The software package SPM12 version 6470 (Wellcome Trust Centre for Neuroimaging, London, UK; http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm) was used to analyse the fMRI data.

claim: Temporal and spatial preprocessing included slice-timing correction, realignment to the mean image, and co-registration to the participant's own structural scan.
source: Temporal and spatial preprocessing included slice-timing correction, realignment to the mean image, and co-registration to the participant's own structural scan.

claim: EPI images were smoothed with an isotropic Gaussian kernel of 6 mm full-width half-maximum.
source: As a final step, EPI images were smoothed with an isotropic Gaussian kernel of 6 mm full-width half-maximum.

claim: BOLD signal fluctuations due to physiological noise were modeled with the PhysIO toolbox using Fourier expansions of different order for the estimated phases of cardiac pulsation (3rd order), respiration (4th order) and cardio-respiratory interactions (1st order).
source: BOLD signal fluctuations due to physiological noise were modeled with the PhysIO toolbox (http://www.translationalneuromodeling.org/tapas) (Kasper et al., 2017) using Fourier expansions of different order for the estimated phases of cardiac pulsation (3rd order), respiration (4th order) and cardio-respiratory interactions (1st order; Glover et al., 2000).
evidence: Direct statement of physiological noise modeling with citations.

claim: The 18 modeled physiological regressors entering the subject-level GLM along with the six rigid-body realignment parameters and regressors of interest were used to account for BOLD signal fluctuations induced by cardiac pulsation, respiration, and the interaction between the two.
source: The 18 modeled physiological regressors entering the subject-level GLM along with the six rigid-body realignment parameters and regressors of interest were used to account for BOLD signal fluctuations induced by cardiac pulsation, respiration, and the interaction between the two.

claim: Arbitration was formalized in terms of hierarchical Bayesian inference as the relative perceived reliability of each information source.
source: We formalized arbitration in terms of hierarchical Bayesian inference as the relative perceived reliability of each information source.
evidence: Direct statement of computational modeling approach.

claim: Arbitration was defined as a ratio of precisions: the precision of the prediction about advice accuracy and color probability, divided by the total precision.
source: In other words, arbitration was defined as a ratio of precisions: the precision of the prediction about advice accuracy and color probability, divided by the total precision.
evidence: Direct statement of computational modeling approach.

claim: The precisions of the predictions afforded by each learning system are obtained by applying a two-branch hierarchical Gaussian filter (HGF) along with a response model to participants' trial-wise behavior (i.e. choices and wagers).
source: The precisions of the predictions afforded by each learning system are obtained by applying a two-branch hierarchical Gaussian filter (Mathys et al., 2011; Mathys et al., 2014) along with a response model (see below) to participants' trial--wise behavior (i.e. choices and wagers).
evidence: Direct statement of computational modeling approach with citations.

claim: The HGF is a model of hierarchical Bayesian inference widely used for computational analyses of behavior.
source: The HGF is a model of hierarchical Bayesian inference widely used for computational analyses of behavior (e.g. [Iglesias et al., 2013; Vossel et al., 2014; Hauser et al., 2014; de Berker et al., 2016; Marshall et al., 2016]).

claim: All models were compared formally using Bayesian model selection (BMS).
source: All models were compared formally using Bayesian model selection (BMS Stephan et al., 2009).
evidence: Direct statement of model comparison method with citation.

claim: Random effects BMS results in a posterior probability for each model given the participants' data.
source: Random effects BMS results in a posterior probability for each model given the participants' data.

claim: The relative goodness of models is denoted by the 'protected exceedance probability' reflecting how likely it is that a given model has a higher posterior probability than any other model in the set of models considered.
source: The relative goodness of models is denoted by the 'protected exceedance probability' reflecting how likely it is that a given model has a higher posterior probability than any other model in the set of models considered (Stephan et al., 2009; Rigoux et al., 2014).

claim: Maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) estimates of model parameters were obtained using the HGF toolbox version 3.0, freely available as part of the open source software package TAPAS at http://www.translationalneuromodeling.org/tapas.
source: Maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) estimates of model parameters were obtained using the HGF toolbox version 3.0, freely available as part of the open source software package TAPAS at http://www.translationalneuromodeling.org/tapas.
evidence: Direct statement of parameter estimation method.

claim: The GLMs were individualized, as the regressors were obtained from fitting the model to the behavioral data of each of the 38 participants.
source: The GLMs were individualized, as the regressors were obtained from fitting the model to the behavioral data of each of the 38 participants.
evidence: Direct statement of fMRI analysis approach.

claim: Parametric modulators were not orthogonalized to investigate the unique contribution of each.
source: To investigate the unique contribution of each parametric modulator, we did not orthogonalize them (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for correlations between them).
evidence: Direct statement of fMRI analysis approach.

claim: Movement and the physiological noise regressors obtained from the PhysIO toolbox based on ECG and respiration recordings were included as regressors of no interest.
source: Moreover, we also included movement and the physiological noise regressors obtained from the PhysIO toolbox (Kasper et al., 2017) based on ECG and respiration recordings as regressors of no interest.
evidence: Direct statement of fMRI analysis approach with citation.

claim: No significant correlations were observed between response times (RTs) and any of the parametric modulators (|r| < 0.3, p>0.05).
source: We observed no significant correlations between response times (RTs) and any of the parametric modulators (|r| < 0.3, p>0.05) and therefore did not model RT explicitly.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: RT was not modeled explicitly because no significant correlations were observed between RTs and parametric modulators.
source: We observed no significant correlations between response times (RTs) and any of the parametric modulators (|r| < 0.3, p>0.05) and therefore did not model RT explicitly.

claim: The lack of effects on RTs may be due to the temporal structure of the task where participants responded long after having received individual information and social information had fixed duration.
source: The lack of effects on RTs may be due to the temporal structure of our task (Figure 1). Specifically, participants responded long after having received individual information (card outcome in previous trial) and social information had fixed duration (video). Therefore, they are likely to have simply conveyed the decision in the response phase but made it at some time during the video or even before.
evidence: Statement providing interpretation of null result.

claim: Contrast images from the 38 participants entered a random effects group analysis.
source: Contrast images from the 38 participants entered a random effects group analysis (Penny and Holmes, 2007).
evidence: Direct statement of group-level analysis with citation.

claim: F-tests were used to identify undirected arbitration signals.
source: We used F-tests to identify undirected arbitration signals.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test used.

claim: One-sample t-tests were used to investigate directed social or individual arbitration signals and positive or negative BOLD responses for each of the computational trajectories of interest.
source: Moreover, one-sample t-tests to investigate directed social or individual arbitration signals and positive or negative BOLD responses for each of the computational trajectories of interest described above.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test used.

claim: Participant gender and age were included as covariates of no interest at the group level.
source: Participant gender and age were included as covariates of no interest at the group level (the findings remained the same without these covariates).

claim: The findings remained the same without gender and age covariates.
source: Participant gender and age were included as covariates of no interest at the group level (the findings remained the same without these covariates).

claim: Results that survived whole-brain family-wise error (FWE) correction at the cluster level at p<0.05, under a cluster-defining threshold of p<0.001 at the voxel level using Gaussian random field theory are reported.
source: For all analyses, we report results that survived whole-brain family-wise error (FWE) correction at the cluster level at p<0.05, under a cluster-defining threshold of p<0.001 at the voxel level using Gaussian random field theory (Worsley et al., 1996).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical threshold with citation.

claim: The cluster-defining threshold of p<0.001 ensures adequate control of cluster-level FWE rates in SPM.
source: Given recent debate regarding the vulnerabilities of cluster-level FWE procedures (Eklund et al., 2016), it is worth emphasising that this cluster-defining threshold ensures adequate control of cluster-level FWE rates in SPM (Flandin and Friston, 2016).

claim: The coordinates of all brain regions were expressed in Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space.
source: The coordinates of all brain regions were expressed in Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space.

claim: ROI analyses were performed based on anatomical masks including (i) the dopaminergic midbrain nuclei substantia nigra (SN) and ventral tegmental area (VTA), (ii) the cholinergic nuclei in the basal forebrain and the tegmentum of the brainstem, and (iii) the noradrenergic locus coeruleus.
source: Based on recent results that precisions at different levels of a computational hierarchy may be encoded by distinct neuromodulatory systems (Payzan-LeNestour et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2015), we also performed ROI analyses based on anatomical masks. We included (i) the dopaminergic midbrain nuclei substantia nigra (SN) and ventral tegmental area (VTA) using an anatomical atlas based on magnetization transfer weighted structural MR images (Bunzeck and Düzel, 2006), (ii) the cholinergic nuclei in the basal forebrain and the tegmentum of the brainstem using the anatomical toolbox in SPM12 with anatomical landmarks from the literature (Naidich and Duvernoy, 2009) and (iii) the noradrenergic locus coeruleus based on a probabilistic map (Keren et al., 2009) (see Figure 8—figure supplement 1 for this neuromodulatory ROI).
evidence: Direct statement of ROI analysis approach with citations.

claim: The routines for all analyses are available as Matlab code at https://github.com/andreeadiaconescu/arbitration.
source: The routines for all analyses are available as Matlab code: https://github.com/andreeadiaconescu/arbitration (Kasper and Diaconescu, 2020; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/arbitration).
